raw_text:
Transcatheter structural heart therapies have progressively moved from rescue treatment to mainstream care, particularly for aortic stenosis [1-6]. Yet safe large-bore access remains the prerequisite for success. Although transfemoral arterial access is preferred, iliofemoral calcification, tortuosity, small caliber, prior endovascular repair, or prohibitive bleeding risk may force alternative strategies. Standardized outcome definitions have helped clarify the burden of access-related bleeding, vascular injury, stroke, acute kidney injury, and mortality [7,8]. Historically, nonfemoral access included transapical, transaortic, subclavian/axillary, carotid, and other surgical or hybrid routes; these approaches can be effective but introduce thoracic trauma, neurologic risk, surgical exposure, or unfavorable catheter ergonomics [9].

Transcaval access is a percutaneous transfemoral venous route to the abdominal aorta. The operator advances equipment from the femoral vein into the inferior vena cava, crosses into the adjacent infrarenal aorta with an electrified guidewire aimed at an aortic snare, exchanges for a stiff wire, and delivers the large-bore sheath retrograde through the aorta. Preclinical work showed that large sheaths could be introduced from the vena cava into the aorta and that the tract could be closed with nitinol occluders, with the key physiologic insight that aortic bleeding can decompress into the low-pressure caval lumen rather than expand freely in the retroperitoneum [10]. The first human series established feasibility in patients otherwise ineligible for TAVR, though transfusion and residual aortocaval fistula were common [11].

Patient selection is anatomy-driven. Contrast CT is used to identify a calcium-free aortic target adjacent to the cava, avoid bowel or critical interposed structures, ensure adequate distance from renal vessels and the aortoiliac bifurcation, and plan bailout covered-stent landing zones [12]. Special situations, including traversal of polyester aortic grafts, have been reported, supporting the concept that transcaval access may be feasible despite prior aortic surgery when imaging is favorable [13]. In the prospective NHLBI transcaval TAVR study, transcaval access succeeded in 99 of 100 subjects, and device success occurred in 98; however, major or life-threatening transcaval-related bleeding remained clinically important, reflecting use of off-label permeable cardiac occluders [14]. One-year follow-up was reassuring: most fistulas closed, no deaths were attributed to transcaval access, and late vascular sequelae were uncommon [15].

Closure is the central technical vulnerability. Commercial Amplatzer duct or muscular ventricular septal defect occluders can seal the tract but are not designed for tangential deployment in the aortic wall. A dedicated transcaval closure device was therefore developed with polyester-covered nitinol discs and features to reduce pull-through; first-in-human testing suggested improved immediate hemostasis and usability [16]. Contemporary best practice emphasizes meticulous CT planning, a right femoral venous large-bore route, arterial access for snaring and bailout, full heparinization before crossing, protamine before closure, a “buddy” wire during occluder deployment, and immediate availability of aortic balloon tamponade and covered stents [17].

Comparative data remain observational. A propensity-weighted multicenter analysis found lower stroke or transient ischemic attack with transcaval than transaxillary TAVR, with similar bleeding and vascular complications, although both nonfemoral strategies had worse outcomes than standard transfemoral access [18]. A smaller single-center comparison of subclavian and transcaval approaches showed broadly comparable intermediate outcomes [19]. Meta-analytic evidence suggests high technical success and acceptable early outcomes, but conclusions are limited by selection bias, heterogeneous operator experience, and small cohorts [20]. Fully percutaneous TAVR programs incorporating transcaval access, transaxillary access, and adjunctive iliofemoral techniques demonstrate that alternative access can be integrated into minimalist pathways when the heart team is experienced [21].

The technique continues to evolve. Reports describe sheathless transcaval TAVI through an abdominal aortic graft [22], transradial secondary access to reduce femoral arterial instrumentation [23], left-sided venous access when right-sided venous anatomy is unsuitable [24], and emergency delivery of large-flow mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock when femoral arteries cannot accommodate Impella 5.0 [25,26]. Beyond structural heart disease, transcaval aortic entry has informed endovascular aortic interventions and endoleak embolization, reinforcing its broader large-bore access rationale [27-29]. Redo transcaval access for redo TAVR has also been described, suggesting that prior transcaval closure need not preclude future intervention in selected anatomy [30].

In summary, transcaval access is no longer merely a bailout curiosity; it is a reproducible, fully percutaneous alternative for structural heart interventions requiring large-bore aortic access when transfemoral arteries are unsuitable. Its strengths are favorable venous entry, transfemoral-like ergonomics, avoidance of thoracotomy, and potentially lower neurologic risk than supra-aortic access. Its limitations are dependence on CT planning, specialized operator training, contrast and fluoroscopy burden, closure-device imperfections, and bleeding risk. Future priorities include broader dissemination of dedicated closure technology, standardized training, registry-based benchmarking, and prospective comparisons with transaxillary, transcarotid, and optimized transfemoral strategies.
